item.title: linux-user-management
item.description:
Scope: Debian-based and RHEL-based Linux distributions
Topics: Regular user creation, system user creation, sudo privileges, verification, and usage scenarios.

Part 1: Debian-Based Systems#

Examples: Debian, Ubuntu

1. Install sudo#

Run as root:

apt update
apt install sudo

2. Create a Regular User#

Create a user interactively:

adduser <USERNAME>

Alternatively, use useradd:

useradd -m -s /bin/bash <USERNAME>
passwd <USERNAME>

Options:

  • -m: Creates the user’s home directory.
  • -s /bin/bash: Sets Bash as the default shell.
  • passwd: Sets or changes the user’s password.

item.title: file-permissions
item.description:
Scope: Distro-independent; applies to ext4, XFS, and other standard Linux filesystems
Topics: ls -l output, ugo and rwx, chmod notation, ownership with chown and chgrp, umask, SUID, SGID, sticky bit, ACLs, and verification.

Main Flow#

1. Read the Permission String#

List the file details:

ls -l <FILE>

Expected output:

-rwxr-xr-- 1 alice devops 2048 Mar  5 10:00 report.sh

Break down the output:

  • -rwxr-xr--: Permission string.
  • 1: Hard link count.
  • alice: Owner (user).
  • devops: Owning group.
  • 2048: Size in bytes.
  • Mar 5 10:00: Last modification time.
  • report.sh: File name.

item.title: sudo
item.description:
Scope: Debian-based and RHEL-based Linux distributions
Topics: sudo basics, visudo, sudoers syntax, command tags, drop-in files, privilege inspection, logging, and common pitfalls.

Part 1: Debian-Based Systems#

Examples: Debian, Ubuntu

1. Install sudo#

Run as root:

apt update
apt install sudo

2. Edit the Sudoers File Safely#

Edit the sudoers configuration only with visudo:

visudo

visudo locks the file against concurrent edits, parses the result before saving, and refuses to write a broken configuration. A single syntax error in /etc/sudoers can remove administrative access from every account.

item.title: ssh
item.description:
Scope: Debian-based and RHEL-based Linux distributions
Topics: ed25519 key pairs, public key installation, authorized_keys permissions, sshd hardening, service validation and restart, and ssh-agent.

Part 1: Debian-Based Systems#

Examples: Debian, Ubuntu

1. Generate an ed25519 Key Pair#

Run on the client machine as the user who will log in:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "<USERNAME>@<CLIENT_HOST>" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Options:

  • -t ed25519: Uses the Ed25519 algorithm. It is fast, small, and current.
  • -C: Attaches a comment to the public key, typically the account and host.
  • -f: Sets the output path for the private key.

Enter a passphrase when prompted. The private key is stored encrypted on disk.

item.title: process-management
item.description:
Scope: Debian-based and RHEL-based Linux distributions
Topics: Process listing, signals, priority, background jobs, zombie diagnosis, and the /proc filesystem.

1. List Running Processes#

List all processes of all users in BSD style:

ps aux

Columns:

  • USER: Owner of the process.
  • PID: Process ID.
  • %CPU and %MEM: CPU and memory usage.
  • VSZ and RSS: Virtual and resident memory in kibibytes.
  • TTY: Controlling terminal. ? means no terminal.
  • STAT: Process state. R running, S sleeping, Z zombie, T stopped.
  • START: Start time of the process.
  • TIME: Accumulated CPU time.
  • COMMAND: Executed command.

item.title: firewall
item.description:
Scope: Debian-based and RHEL-based Linux distributions
Topics: Host firewalls, ufw, application profiles, firewalld, zones, rich rules, nftables, iptables, common ports, and safe rule management.

A host firewall filters incoming and outgoing traffic on a single system. It is the first control point for exposed services and should be configured before a service is started on a production interface. Debian-based systems commonly use ufw, RHEL-based systems use firewalld, and both build their rules on the nftables kernel framework.

1. Work Through the Layers#

Diagnose in a fixed order: link, address, route, DNS, port, then application. Stop at the first failing layer and fix it before continuing. Skipping layers produces false conclusions and wasted time.

item.title: filesystem-hierarchy
item.description:
Scope: Standard Linux filesystem hierarchy on Debian-based and RHEL-based distributions
Topics: FHS directory layout, /bin vs /sbin, virtual filesystems, mount points, safe cleanup, and reference tables.

1. Understand the Root Directory#

The root directory / is the single top of the filesystem tree. Every file and device on the system is reachable from it.

Inspect it:

ls /

Expected output (contents vary by installation):

bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  lib64  media  mnt  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var

The layout follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS). Each directory holds a specific category of data: configuration in /etc, variable data in /var, user data in /home, and virtual kernel interfaces in /proc, /sys, and /dev.

item.title: lvm
item.description:
Scope: Logical Volume Management on Debian-based and RHEL-based distributions
Topics: PV, VG, LV, pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, lvextend, resize2fs, xfs_growfs, cloud volume extension.

1. Understand the LVM Model#

LVM places an abstraction layer between physical disks and filesystems:

  • Physical Volume (PV): A disk or partition registered with LVM.
  • Volume Group (VG): A storage pool built from one or more PVs.
  • Logical Volume (LV): A flexible volume carved from a VG, formatted and mounted like a partition.

An LV appears as /dev/<VG_NAME>/<LV_NAME>. Unlike partitions, LVs can be extended while mounted.

item.title: disk-troubleshooting
item.description:
Scope: Diagnosing and resolving full-filesystem and inode exhaustion on Debian-based and RHEL-based distributions
Topics: df, du, inodes, deleted-but-open files, lsof, log growth, package caches, containers.

1. Check Space Usage with df#

Start with the filesystem that reports high usage:

df -h
df -hT

Expected output (example):

Filesystem     Type  Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda2      ext4   50G   48G  2.0G  96% /

Options:

  • -h: Human-readable sizes.
  • -T: Adds the filesystem type.

A full filesystem fails writes with No space left on device. Note the mount point: a full /var can stop services while / still has free space.

item.title: log-management
item.description:
Scope: Log sources, locations, querying, and rotation on Debian-based and RHEL-based distributions
Topics: rsyslog, /var/log layout, journald, journalctl, logrotate.

1. Understand the Log Sources#

Two logging systems handle messages on current distributions:

  • systemd-journald: Collects messages from the kernel, services, and stdout/stderr of units. Stores them in the journal, which is volatile in /run/log/journal unless persistent storage is configured.
  • rsyslog: Traditional syslog daemon. Reads /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf and writes text files under /var/log. On RHEL-based systems it imports messages from the journal through the imjournal module.

item.title: selinux-apparmor
item.description:
Scope: Mandatory access control on RHEL-based and Debian-based Linux distributions
Topics: SELinux modes, file contexts, booleans, denial analysis, AppArmor profiles, troubleshooting.

Traditional Unix permissions implement discretionary access control (DAC): the file owner decides who may read, write, or execute a resource. Mandatory access control (MAC) adds a system-wide policy that restricts programs to only the resources they are explicitly allowed to use, regardless of file ownership. SELinux enforces MAC with labels on processes and objects, while AppArmor enforces it with path-based profiles.

item.title: security-hardening
item.description:
Scope: Debian-based and RHEL-based Linux server hardening
Topics: Baseline hardening, fail2ban, automatic security updates, listening ports, login auditing.

Server hardening reduces the attack surface before an incident occurs: keep the system patched, expose only required services, restrict administrative access, and monitor authentication attempts. Fail2ban complements these measures by banning hosts that repeatedly fail authentication. Treat the steps below as a baseline and adjust them to the role of each server.

Topics: Package installation, removal, upgrades, repository management, version locking, and low-level package tools.

Part 1: Debian-Based Systems#

Examples: Debian, Ubuntu

1. Refresh the Package Index#

Run as root before installing or upgrading:

2. Install Packages#

  • -y: Confirms all prompts automatically. Use only in scripts and after reviewing the transaction.
  • --no-install-recommends: Installs hard dependencies only, skipping recommended packages.
  • --dry-run: Simulates the transaction without changing the system.

item.description:
Scope: Distro-independent performance triage on Linux servers
Topics: Load average, CPU versus I/O wait, memory and swap pressure, disk I/O, culprit processes.

Performance triage answers one question first: is the system CPU-bound, memory-bound, or I/O-bound? Measure before changing anything, because tuning the wrong resource hides the real bottleneck. The workflow below uses tools available on Debian-based and RHEL-based systems alike.

1. Read the Load Average#

Inspect the load average:

item.title: boot-process
item.description:
Scope: Boot chain, systemd targets, and GRUB configuration on Debian-based and RHEL-based systems
Topics: UEFI and GRUB, kernel and initramfs, systemd targets, boot timing, kernel parameters, boot recovery.

A Linux server boots through a fixed chain: the firmware (UEFI or BIOS) starts the GRUB 2 bootloader, GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs, the kernel hands control to systemd, systemd reaches the default target, and a login prompt appears. Each stage fails in a distinct way, so knowing the chain narrows a boot problem quickly. The steps below cover diagnosis first, then GRUB configuration per distribution family, then recovery.
